%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the

\begin{abstract}
  Deciding where a small group should meet for dinner or a casual outing is a routine coordination task that today's tools handle poorly: map and food-discovery apps are built for one searcher at a time, so the group reconciles by hand. We present MeetHalfway, an interactive geospatial demo for everyday small-group meeting-place recommendation. A single room collects each participant's origin, travel mode (walking, driving, transit), commute budget, and venue preference; the system computes per-participant reachable regions, extracts the shared feasible region, retrieves candidate venues, estimates per-participant travel effort, and ranks candidates with a mode-aware equity score that pulls the recommendation toward participants on slower modes rather than the geometric centroid. For each top venue, a lightweight context module turns web-search snippets into a short structured status note (open/closed, queue level, wait estimate, brief reason) via a temperature-zero JSON-constrained LLM call with a keyword fallback. Attendees inspect each recommendation through a card exposing per-participant travel effort, score components, contextual signals, and whether the result satisfies strict shared reachability or is a relaxed alternative.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Imagine four colleagues finishing work in different parts of a city and trying to share a coffee. One drives, one takes a bus, one walks, one comes from downtown; each has a different patience for travel. They want a real cafe that everyone can reach with comparable effort---rarely the geometric midpoint of the group. Today this is usually settled by everyone searching on Yelp or Google Maps separately and reconciling by hand: a small but recurring everyday coordination cost.

The literature touches related problems but not this one. Aggregate nearest-neighbor and optimal-meeting-point queries on road networks minimize SUM, MAX, or MIN aggregation of network distance from a fixed set of starts~\cite{papadias2005ann,yan2011omp,kim2023meeting}; optimal-sequenced-route group-meetup queries assume each participant first visits a sequence of category-typed errands before converging~\cite{chen2021groupmeetup}; envy-free group trip planning enforces pairwise distance-disparity bounds among participants as a hard constraint~\cite{singhal2022envyfree}; pre-event meeting-point recommenders dispatch attendees to nearby train stations to relieve congestion around event venues~\cite{asukai2018meeting}; ride-sharing meeting-point GIS work places interurban pickup spots~\cite{czioska2017gis,czioska2017location,khetarpaul2012mining}; and POI recommenders~\cite{sanchez2022poi,liu2013poi,wang2024embracing} suggest venues from a single user's preferences. Group venue recommendation has been studied with mobility traces and social weights~\cite{zhang2019gevr} and with diversification objectives~\cite{dacruz2024diversification}; group-fairness aggregation has been formalized as a relevance-minus-disagreement objective for non-spatial recommender settings~\cite{ameryahia2009group,stratigi2020fair,wang2023fairness}. These works each cover part of the problem but not the everyday interactive case where a room of friends each enters origin, travel mode, and venue preference \emph{now} under heterogeneous mode-and-budget constraints and expects a ranked list of real, reachable venues with a per-candidate explanation.

We present MeetHalfway, an interactive geospatial demo for everyday small-group meeting-place recommendation. A shared room collects every participant's origin, travel mode (walking, driving, transit), commute budget, and venue preference. From these, MeetHalfway computes per-participant isochrone reachable regions, extracts their shared feasible region, retrieves real candidate venues inside it, estimates per-participant travel effort, and ranks candidates with a mode-aware fairness-aware score that pulls the recommendation closer to participants on slower modes (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}). A lightweight context module then turns web-search snippets for each top candidate into a short structured status note, so a user can read a brief venue summary without leaving the interface.

This paper contributes (i) a \emph{room-based collective input interface} that replaces the everyone-searches-Yelp-separately status quo with one shared form for daily small-group coordination; (ii) an \emph{isochrone-intersection pipeline with mode-aware fairness} and an explicit strict-vs.-relaxed feasibility status when the strict shared region collapses; and (iii) an \emph{explainable interface} that exposes the shared reachable region, per-participant travel effort, the score components, and the strict-vs.-relaxed feasibility status for every ranked venue.



\section{System Overview}
\label{sec:overview}

\noindent\textbf{User workflow.} A session begins when one user creates a meeting room and shares its link. Each participant enters their own \emph{starting location}, \emph{travel mode} (walking, driving, transit), \emph{commute budget} (a travel-cost limit interpreted as a distance or time threshold), and \emph{venue preference} (cafe, restaurant, library, etc.); the room carries group-level context---a shared venue category and an ambiance preference (quiet/balanced/lively). This keeps the workflow symmetric: no single user controls everyone's constraints.

\noindent\textbf{Interface and explanation.} On submission, a single map canvas shows each participant's starting location and reachable region, the shared feasible region (their intersection), candidate venues, and the ranked recommendations; a side panel lists the ranking. Selecting a venue opens an explanation card with participant-level travel effort, the four score components from Section~\ref{sec:rank}, contextual venue signals (rating from the POI API; mutual venue votes and time-slot overlap from participant inputs; open status, queue level, and wait estimate distilled by the LLM from web-search snippets), and whether the result satisfies strict shared reachability or is a relaxed alternative. The same card carries a short \emph{context note} per top candidate: web-search snippets from a Tavily query are passed to an LLM that emits a structured JSON record (open status, queue level, crowd index, wait estimate, one-sentence reason, confidence) at temperature zero, with a keyword-matching fallback. The note is an auxiliary status summary, not a ranking driver; the JSON schema, confidence field, and fallback bound hallucination risk.

\noindent\textbf{Architecture.} Figure~\ref{fig:arch} shows the frontend--backend design. The frontend collects the query, renders the visualization layers above, and displays the explanation card. The backend engine returns ranked candidates with the supporting data---per-participant travel costs, score components, strict/relaxed status, visualization geometry---through the five-stage pipeline of Section~\ref{sec:pipeline}, using external routing and place-search services with service-specific fall-backs rather than failing the workflow.

\section{Recommendation Pipeline}
\label{sec:pipeline}

This section describes how MeetHalfway computes a ranked list of candidate meeting places. Let $U = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n\}$ denote the set of participants ($n \geq 2$). For each participant $u_i$, the system records a starting location $s_i$, a travel mode $m_i$, and a \emph{travel-cost budget} $\phi_i$. The travel cost is a generalized scalar threshold whose unit is selected once per query and applied to all participants; depending on the user setting, it is instantiated as a travel-time limit (minutes) or a travel-distance limit (miles). We write $\rho(s_i, x, m_i)$ for the corresponding travel cost from $s_i$ to a location $x$ under mode $m_i$, as returned by the external routing service. The pipeline proceeds through five stages.

\subsection{Isochrone Generation}
\label{sec:iso}

For each participant $u_i$, the system computes a reachable region $I_i$, the set of locations whose routing-service cost from $s_i$ does not exceed $\phi_i$:
\begin{equation}
  I_i \;=\; \{\, x : \rho(s_i, x, m_i) \leq \phi_i \,\}.
  \label{eq:isochrone}
\end{equation}
$I_i$ is realized as the road-network polygon returned by the OpenRouteService isochrone for mode $m_i$ at threshold $\phi_i$, using either its distance or time isochrone endpoint depending on the active travel-cost unit. Because each participant can use a different mode and budget, $I_i$ is computed independently; participants with larger budgets or faster modes contribute larger reachable regions. When the routing service is unavailable, the system falls back to a mode-aware ellipsoidal buffer around $s_i$ sized so that its on-the-ground radius matches $\phi_i$ under the active travel-cost unit; the fall-back is logged on the server side and rendered identically to a real isochrone in the map view.

\subsection{Shared Feasible Region}
\label{sec:region}

Individual reachable regions are converted to a group-level feasibility set by polygon intersection. The strict shared feasible region is
\begin{equation}
  R \;=\; \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} I_i .
  \label{eq:intersection}
\end{equation}
A location inside $R$ is reachable by every participant under the current constraints. When $R \neq \emptyset$, the pipeline runs in \emph{strict mode}, retrieving candidates inside $R$. When $R = \emptyset$, it switches to \emph{relaxed mode}: the search space is broadened to $\bigcup_i I_i$, and every candidate that violates one or more participants' budgets is tagged for the relaxation penalty in Section~\ref{sec:rank}. The strict/relaxed status is surfaced in the explanation card so the user sees the degradation explicitly rather than receiving a silent fall-back.

\subsection{POI Retrieval}
\label{sec:poi}

Within the active region---$R$ in strict mode, $\bigcup_i I_i$ in relaxed mode---the system retrieves a candidate set $C = \{c_1, \ldots, c_k\}$ via three filters. \emph{Spatial filtering} keeps POIs whose coordinates lie inside the active region. \emph{Semantic filtering} keeps only POIs matching the requested category, removing reachable-but-irrelevant places. \emph{Multi-source retrieval} queries Foursquare Places, the Mapbox Geocoding/POI API, OpenStreetMap Overpass, and Nominatim in turn so the candidate set degrades gracefully when one source returns too few results. If the strict filter empties $C$ (small $R$ or sparse local POI density), it is bypassed conservatively and candidates are re-ranked by distance to the centroid of $R$, with the bypass surfaced in the explanation so imbalance appears as a low equity score rather than a silent failure.

\subsection{Travel-Effort Estimation}
\label{sec:rte}

Travel cost plays two roles. \emph{Absolute} reachability is gated by Equation~\eqref{eq:isochrone}: the OpenRouteService isochrone $I_i$ encodes the road-network cost $\rho(s_i, x, m_i)$, so the spatial filter of Section~\ref{sec:poi} cannot let a candidate the routing service deems unreachable for participant $i$ enter the ranking stage. For the \emph{relative} per-(participant, candidate) effort that drives mode-aware ranking and the explanation card, we compute
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf{T}_j \;=\; \bigl(T_{1,j}, \ldots, T_{n,j}\bigr), \qquad
  T_{i,j} \;=\; \hat{t}(s_i, c_j, m_i),
  \label{eq:tvec}
\end{equation}
where $\hat{t}$ is the great-circle distance from $s_i$ to $c_j$ divided by a per-mode reference speed (walking $5$, driving $40$, transit $20$\,km/h). $\hat{t}$ is a deliberate proxy: a routing API call per (participant, candidate) pair would cost $O(n \cdot |C|)$ external calls and break the free-tier quota; the proxy holds routing at $O(n)$ per query while staying mode-specific, so the equity term still pulls ranking toward slow-mode participants (Section~\ref{sec:rank}). The road-network gate still prevents recommending unreachable candidates; a batched ORS/Mapbox matrix call over the filtered $|C|$ is the production-tier upgrade, and the explanation card surfaces displayed times as estimates.

\subsection{Fairness-Aware Ranking}
\label{sec:rank}

Candidates are ranked by a composite score combining a participant-level commute-equity term, venue suitability, contextual venue signals, and a relaxation penalty:
\begin{equation}
  S(c_j) \;=\; \alpha\, E(c_j) + \beta\, V(c_j) + \gamma\, C(c_j) - \delta\, P(c_j),
  \label{eq:score}
\end{equation}
where each component is min-max normalized to $[0,1]$ before weighting so the terms are scale-comparable, and the weights $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are non-negative. The \emph{Commute Equity Term} $E$ is a clipped, gap-based metric of participant travel-effort balance:
\begin{equation}
  E(c_j) \;=\; \max\!\Bigl(0,\; 1 - \tfrac{\max_i T_{i,j} - \min_i T_{i,j}}{G_{\mathrm{ref}}(c_j)}\Bigr),
  \label{eq:fair}
\end{equation}
with $G_{\mathrm{ref}}(c_j) = \sum_i T_{i,j}$, so the same absolute gap counts as a larger imbalance among short trips than among long ones. $E$ itself is mode-agnostic; mode-awareness enters through $T_{i,j}$, already normalized by mode $m_i$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:tvec}, so slower-mode participants contribute larger $T$ and the $E$-maximizer shifts toward them. Absolute travel burden is bounded above by each per-participant budget $\phi_i$ and pushed down by the centrality term $D$ below. \emph{Venue suitability} $V$ combines a rating proxy with a crowd-density balance term that penalizes both over- and under-crowded venues. \emph{Contextual venue signal} $C$ is itself a normalized weighted sum of sub-signals: centrality $D(c_j)=\max(0,1-d_{\mathrm{center}}(c_j)/d_{\max})$ (with $d_{\mathrm{center}}$ the haversine distance to the commute-tolerance-weighted participant centroid), an ambiance-target term $A(c_j)$ tied to the room's quiet/balanced/lively preference $\tau$, an isochrone-intersection indicator, and soft participant-input signals (mutual venue votes, time-slot availability overlap, shared time-slot votes), each clipped to $[0,1]$ with its own sub-weight and surfaced per-candidate in the explanation card. Open/closed status and wait-time estimates from web snippets attenuate $C$ as soft penalties; venues whose status is confirmed closed are removed before ranking rather than down-weighted. \emph{Relaxation penalty} $P(c_j)=0$ for $c_j \in R$, and grows with budget violations in relaxed mode; subtracting $\delta P(c_j)$ deprioritizes relaxed candidates without removing them. Algorithm~\ref{alg:rank} evaluates $S(c_j)$ in the form used by the prototype.

Relative to prior work, $E$ is a soft min-max relaxation of the MAX-aggregate ANN objective~\cite{papadias2005ann} and a soft, additive analogue of the hard envy-free distance-disparity bound~\cite{singhal2022envyfree}, blended with relevance-like terms in the relevance-minus-disagreement style~\cite{ameryahia2009group} so the system still returns a ranked list when no perfectly equitable candidate exists.

\begin{algorithm}[!htbp]
\small
\caption{Fairness-aware ranking}
\label{alg:rank}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require candidates $C$, participants $U$, shared region $R$
\Require weights $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta)$ and sub-weights $(w_D, w_K, w_A)$, ambiance target $\tau$
\For{each candidate $c_j \in C$}
  \State $\mathbf{T}_j \gets \bigl(\hat{t}(s_i, c_j, m_i)\bigr)_{i=1}^{n}$
  \State $\mathrm{gap}(c_j) \gets \max_i T_{i,j} - \min_i T_{i,j}$
  \State $G_{\mathrm{ref}}(c_j) \gets \max\!\bigl(\sum_i T_{i,j},\, \epsilon\bigr)$
  \State $E(c_j) \gets \max\!\bigl(0, 1 - \mathrm{gap}(c_j)/G_{\mathrm{ref}}(c_j)\bigr)$
  \State $V(c_j) \gets \mathrm{suitability}(c_j)$
  \State $D(c_j) \gets \max\!\bigl(0, 1 - d_{\mathrm{center}}(c_j)/d_{\max}\bigr)$
  \State $k \gets \mathrm{crowd\_index}(c_j)$
  \State $K(c_j) \gets \max(0, 1-k);\;\; A(c_j) \gets \max\!\bigl(0, 1 - |k-\tau|/0.85\bigr)$
  \State $C(c_j) \gets w_D D(c_j) + w_K K(c_j) + w_A A(c_j)$
  \State $P(c_j) \gets 0$ if $c_j \in R$ else relaxation penalty for budget violations
  \State $S(c_j) \gets \alpha E(c_j) + \beta V(c_j) + \gamma C(c_j) - \delta P(c_j)$
\EndFor
\State \Return $C$ sorted in descending order of $S$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The deployed demo uses default high-level weights $\alpha=0.30$, $\beta=0.22$, $\gamma=0.48$, $\delta=1.0$ for the four-term composition of Equation~\eqref{eq:score}, hand-tuned on a small development set; $V$ and $C$ decompose into the normalized sub-signals described above (rating, density balance, centrality $D$, ambiance fit $A$, isochrone membership, mutual votes, time-slot overlap, and time-slot votes), whose sub-weights are fixed at deploy time and surfaced per-candidate in the explanation card. Setting $\delta=1.0$ ensures strictly feasible candidates dominate relaxed ones at equal $E,V,C$.

\caption{S1, captured live from the SIGSPATIAL\,2026 attendee scenario: three colleagues at three conference-area hotels in Riverside enter one room. The pipeline returns five reachable restaurants ranked by mode-aware fairness and venue suitability, each annotated with a short structured context note from a Tavily web search.}
\Description{Two stacked screenshots from the live MeetHalfway demo. The top panel shows a downtown Riverside map with three participant pins and several ranked-venue pins clustered nearby. The bottom panel shows the top venue's recommendation card with AI score, fairness gap, reputation, crowd index, a context note, the per-term score breakdown, and a nearby-parking link.}
\label{fig:scenarios}

The demo opens on the result page (Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios}), captured live at \url{localhost:8502/?demo_seed=sigspatial2026}; the interface follows Section~\ref{sec:overview}.

\noindent\textbf{S1. Mixed travel modes.} Three attendees at different conference-area Riverside hotels (Marriott on Market\,St, Mission Inn, Hampton Inn near UCR) each pick their own mode---walking, transit, driving---and budget. Their reachable regions differ markedly in shape; guided by the mode-aware equity rule of Section~\ref{sec:rank}, the ranking favors candidates accommodating the slowest-mode participant rather than the geometric centroid.

\noindent\textbf{S2. No strict shared region (relaxed mode).} Two participants start far apart with tight budgets, so no strict shared region exists. The system switches to relaxed mode and broadens the search range (Section~\ref{sec:region}); the interface labels the constraint as relaxed and, per candidate, displays which budgets are exceeded, making the effect of $P(c_j)$ visible.


\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We demonstrate fair, explainable, group-aware meeting-place recommendation combining shared reachability, multi-source POI retrieval, per-participant travel-effort estimation, and an equity-aware ranking with strict/relaxed feasibility status in one interactive demo.
